name: Phthalo Green
lede: Phthalo green is a modern synthetic green pigment, deep, cool and intense, first made in the 20th century.

sections.title: A twentieth-century pigment
sections.body:
Coles dates the phthalo pigments to the early 20th century, the first organic colorants to be called true pigments [1]. Until then, organic pigments such as madder and cochineal had started life as dyes or lakes and were converted afterward [1]. The phthalos have enormous tinting strength, lightfastness and chemical resistance, and they quickly came to dominate the blue and green pigment markets [1].

Coles describes phthalo green as a deep, cool, emerald green, and phthalo blue as almost pure chromatic blue with no lean toward red or green [1]. In his history of green, the 20th century brought phthalo green, whose gem-like intensity restored green's link to life and vitality [2]. The same chapter notes that copper-and-arsenic greens of the late 18th century poisoned thousands [2].

sections.title: On the shelf
sections.body: St Clair's glossary calls phthalo green a piney blue-green, after a synthetic pigment, and notes that the blue version is sometimes sold as Monastral [3]. Names like these are paint-tube names: the same chemistry yields a range from blue-green to yellow-green, so the word fixes a family, not one shade [1][3]. The swatch here, #123524, is a very dark green; the pure pigment, thinned out, is far brighter [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive of 23,781 paintings has colors near this swatch in 98, or 0.41%, as photographed [5]. The earliest is dated 1460 and the group peaks in the 1900s, at 3.5 times the baseline [5]. Gauguin is the most devoted painter, in 5 of his 50 works here [5]. The pre-1900 matches cannot be phthalo: the pigment did not exist, so the match is a look-alike hue in aged paint and varnish, never a pigment test [1][5].

aka: Monastral green (a brand name for the family)

openers: Phthalo green is a 20th-century invention, so any older painting that matches it is only a look-alike.

issues: Removed claim that phthalo green came 'after' the arsenic greens as a causal sequence; Coles gives two separate statements.
